t: The Luddites were not opposed to machines as such, and many were skilled machine operators; they attacked the machines of manufacturers who were circumventing the standard labour practices of the time.
Each region wrecked the machines that threatened its own trade: wide knitting frames in the Midlands, steam-powered looms in the North West, and shearing frames and gig mills in Yorkshire.
The government answered with 12,000 troops, made machine-breaking a capital crime in 1812 and staged a mass trial at York in 1813, whose executions and transportations quickly ended the movement.
dyk: The Yorkshire croppers broke the cropping machines made by Enoch Taylor of Marsden with a hammer they called “Enoch”, purportedly shouting, “Enoch made them, and Enoch shall break them.”
ev: The Luddite movement begins at Arnold, Nottinghamshire, and spreads rapidly through England
Lord Byron condemns the repression of the textile workers in a speech in the House of Lords
The Destruction of Stocking Frames, etc. Act makes machine-breaking a capital crime
A mass trial at York charges over 60 men; the sentences of execution and transportation quickly end the movement
Activists smash Heathcote’s lace-making machine in Loughborough
Jeremiah Brandreth, a probable ex-Luddite, leads the Pentrich Rising
The Swing Riots in southern and eastern England, an agricultural variant of Luddism, break threshing machines
A Second Luddite Congress at Barnesville, Ohio, issues a manifesto of neo-Luddism

f.where: England: Nottinghamshire and the Midlands, beginning at Arnold near Nottingham; the West Riding of Yorkshire, around Huddersfield, Marsden and Cleckheaton; Lancashire and the North West, at Middleton and Westhoughton; Loughborough in 1816
f.period: begins at Arnold, 11 March 1811; Nottinghamshire from November 1811; the West Riding in early 1812; Lancashire; the York trial, January 1813; last raids in 1816; the Pentrich Rising of 1817, sometimes seen as the last major Luddite act
f.figures: “Ned Ludd”, the legendary weaver or apprentice whose name signed their letters; George Mellor, who led the killing of the mill owner William Horsfall; Jeremiah Brandreth, a probable ex-Luddite who led the Pentrich Rising; Lord Byron, their defender in the House of Lords
f.outcome: suppressed by 12,000 troops, a law making machine-breaking a capital crime and the York trials, whose sentences of execution and transportation quickly ended the movement; the name later came to mean anyone opposed to new technology
